title: 26 — Design a Payment System
html:
26 — Design a Payment System

The one idea: with money, correctness beats latency. Every request carries an idempotency key so retries never double-charge; every money movement is recorded in a double-entry ledger that always balances; and a nightly reconciliation against the payment provider's settlement files catches whatever the online path got wrong.

Step 1 — Scope

  • Backend of an e-commerce marketplace: pay-in (customer → platform) and pay-out (platform → sellers).
  • Card processing via a third-party PSP (Stripe, Adyen…) — we never store raw card data (PCI DSS).
  • 1M transactions/day ≈ 10 TPS — throughput is not the challenge.
  • Reliability, fault tolerance, and reconciliation between internal services and external providers.

Step 2 — High-level design

Pay-in flow

---
title: Payment system — pay-in flow
---
flowchart LR
    U["User checkout"] --> PS["Payment service"]
    PS --> RC["Risk check"]
    PS --> PE["Payment executor"] --> PSP["PSP"] --> Card["Card schemes"]
    PS --> W["Wallet<br/>(merchant balances)"]
    PS --> L["Ledger<br/>(double entry)"]
    PS --> PDB[("Payment DB<br/>payment_event, payment_order")]
  1. User places an order → payment event (one checkout) with one or more payment orders (one per seller).
  2. Payment service stores the event, runs a risk check (AML/fraud, often a third party).
  3. Payment executor executes each order through the PSP.
  4. On success: update wallet (seller balance) and ledger.

Data model

payment_event  (checkout_id PK, buyer_info, seller_info, credit_card_info(token), is_payment_done)
payment_order  (payment_order_id PK, buyer_account, amount DECIMAL/string, currency,
                checkout_id, payment_order_status, ledger_updated, wallet_updated)

⚠️ Never use floating point for money — store as decimal / integer minor units (cents) / string.

payment_order_status: NOT_STARTED → EXECUTING → SUCCESS | FAILED.

Double-entry ledger

Every transaction is recorded as two (or more) entries whose sum is zero:

Account Debit Credit
Buyer $1
Seller $1

End-to-end traceability and auditability; any imbalance is a bug.

Hosted payment page

The PSP hosts the card form (iframe/redirect) so card numbers never touch our servers — hugely reduces PCI scope. We register the payment with the PSP (passing our UUID as the idempotency key), get a token, render the PSP page, and receive the result via redirect + webhook.

Pay-out flow

Same structure; a pay-out provider (e.g. Tipalti, Payoneer, bank transfer) moves money from the platform's account to sellers.

Step 3 — Deep dive

3.1 PSP integration

  • Our backend creates a payment registration with the PSP including a nonce/UUID → gets a token.
  • PSP returns status asynchronously via webhook — verify signature, handle duplicates and out-of-order delivery.

3.2 Reconciliation

Services talk asynchronously; messages can be lost or processed twice. Reconciliation is the safety net: every night the PSP sends a settlement file; we compare it to the ledger.

Mismatch type Handling
Classifiable, automatable Automated fix (well-understood cause)
Classifiable, not automatable Job queue for the finance team
Unclassifiable Special queue, investigated manually

3.3 Handling payment processing delays

Some payments take hours/days (manual risk review, 3-D Secure). Return PENDING to the client, show status in UI, and notify via webhook/polling when resolved.

3.4 Communication between internal services

  • Synchronous HTTP is simple but couples availability (one slow service stalls checkout).
  • Asynchronous via Kafka: payment event published once, consumed by wallet, ledger, analytics, billing independently ✅ for side effects.

3.5 Handling failed payments

  • Track payment state durably (append-only).
  • Retry queue for retryable errors (transient), dead-letter queue for failures that keep failing — investigate.
  • Retry with exponential backoff + jitter; cap attempts.

3.6 Exactly-once = at-least-once + at-most-once

  • At-least-once: retries until success.
  • At-most-once: idempotency — the client sends an Idempotency-Key header (UUID). The server stores the key with a unique constraint; a second request with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again. Same key goes to the PSP.
  • Scenario: user double-clicks "Pay" → same key → one charge. Scenario: PSP succeeded but the response was lost → retry with same key → PSP returns original result.

3.7 Consistency

  • Internal services: exactly-once processing + reconciliation.
  • Between us and the PSP: idempotency + reconciliation.
  • DB replicas: read from the primary for payment status (or use consensus-based stores) to avoid stale reads.

3.8 Security

HTTPS everywhere; request signing and webhooks verification; tokenisation (no raw PANs); rate limiting; DDoS protection; fraud detection (address verification, CVV, behaviour analysis); PCI DSS compliance.

Step 4 — Wrap-up

Idempotency, ledger, reconciliation, async side effects with retry/DLQ, and PSP-hosted card pages. Further topics: monitoring (success rate by PSP, latency), alerting, currency exchange, geography-specific payment methods, cash payments, Google/Apple Pay.

.NET / Azure mapping

  • Money type: decimal in C#, DECIMAL(19,4) in SQL; or a Money value object (amount in minor units + ISO currency).
  • Idempotency: ASP.NET Core middleware/filter reading Idempotency-Key; an IdempotencyRecords table (Key PK, request hash, response status/body, created_at) inserted in the same transaction as the payment row; replay the stored response on repeat.
  • Ledger: an append-only LedgerEntries table (TransactionId, AccountId, Debit, Credit) with a check that each transaction sums to zero; SQL Server ledger tables add cryptographic tamper-evidence.
  • Async side effects: transactional outbox (EF Core + background publisher, or MassTransit's EF outbox) → Service Bus topics; consumers use an inbox table for dedupe.
  • Webhooks: verify the PSP signature (e.g. Stripe's EventUtility.ConstructEvent), store the event ID to dedupe.
  • Resilience: Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience (retry with jitter, circuit breaker, timeout) on PSP calls — but only retry with the same idempotency key.
  • Secrets/keys: Key Vault; reconciliation jobs as scheduled Azure Functions / Container Apps jobs.

Review checklist

  • Pay-in and pay-out flows; payment event vs payment order.
  • Money as decimal/minor units, never float.
  • Double-entry ledger.
  • PSP-hosted payment page (PCI scope).
  • Idempotency keys end to end, including to the PSP.
  • Retry queue + DLQ; reconciliation with settlement files.
